prompt: What is the main job of people in an evaluation of a model in production?

choices.text: Grading every reply the judge failed during the week
choices.why: That is a targeted sample for fixing, not the main job.

choices.text: Replacing the judge on the criteria it finds hard
choices.why: People are too slow to grade traffic at volume.

choices.text: Setting the standard the judge is measured against
choices.why: Right. People cannot grade a week; they can grade sixty replies carefully.

choices.text: Writing the replies the assistant should have given
choices.why: That is building an evaluation set, lesson 13.

prompt: Why did the people label the evaluation set's replies rather than traces from the week?

choices.text: The week's traces hold no question text
choices.why: app.question is on every root span.

choices.text: A question in the set has an id that stays
choices.why: Right. A label still names the same reply after the model or the judge changes.

choices.text: Traces cannot be shown to people at all
choices.why: They can, redacted; annotation queues do exactly that.

choices.text: The evaluation set's replies are shorter to read
choices.why: Length was not the reason.

prompt: Which come out of a round of human labelling, as the lesson describes it? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A measure of how far the judge can be trusted
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Reference labels kept by id
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A better rubric
choices.why: Right. Disagreements are questions the rubric did not answer.

choices.text: A cheaper judge model
choices.why: Labels measure a judge; they do not make one.

prompt: Why does the rubric ask for pass or fail rather than a score from 1 to 5?

choices.text: Kappa cannot be computed on more than two labels
choices.why: Kappa works for any number of categories.

choices.text: judge-1 answers pass or fail, and the people have to match it
choices.why: The rubric is written for people first.

choices.text: Scores take longer to store
choices.why: Storage plays no part.

choices.text: Two people place one reply a point apart without disagreeing
choices.why: Right. A binary verdict asks one question, and a disagreement on it is real.

prompt: What does every line of data/labels.jsonl carry, besides the label?

choices.text: The case, the release, the rubric and the rater
choices.why: Right. The rubric's version matters as much as the reply's id.

choices.text: The trace id of the reply and the time the label was written
choices.why: Labels name the reply by question and release, not by trace.

choices.text: The full reply and its sources
choices.why: Those are in the runs, joined by id.

choices.text: The judge's score beside the person's
choices.why: The judge's verdicts are written apart.

prompt: A label written against version 1 of a rubric may not be mixed with labels written against version ___.
Why is the share of replies two raters agree on not enough on its own?

choices.text: Part of it is free, set by each rater's share of passes
choices.why: Right. Kappa takes the free part away.

choices.text: It is skewed by the length of the replies the raters read
choices.why: Length does not enter.

choices.text: It depends on which rater is listed first
choices.why: Agreement is symmetric.

choices.text: It is always lower than kappa
choices.why: Kappa is at most the agreement, usually well below it.

prompt: Observed agreement 0.6, agreement by chance 0.5. What is kappa?
Ana and Bruno disagreed on 29 replies under version 1. What were 24 of them?

choices.text: Replies about express delivery
choices.why: Those were two of the other five.

choices.text: Replies with no citation in them
choices.why: Every answered reply here is cited; citations are not relevance.

choices.text: The agreed refusal
choices.why: Right. One read the sentence as 'about the question', the other as 'answers it'.

choices.text: Replies from the new release only
choices.why: Both releases refuse, the new one more often.

prompt: What did a kappa of 0.11 between Ana and Bruno say?

choices.text: That one of the two was careless
choices.why: Both readings were reasonable.

choices.text: That the labels could not serve as a reference
choices.why: Right. It says nothing about the replies and everything about the rubric.

choices.text: That the replies were mostly irrelevant
choices.why: Kappa measures the raters, not the replies.

choices.text: That the judge should replace them
choices.why: A judge measured against these labels would be measured against a coin.

prompt: What is an anchor in a rubric?

choices.text: The threshold the judge uses to pass a reply
choices.why: That is judge-1's rule, not part of the rubric.

choices.text: The first label each rater writes
choices.why: Order plays no part.

choices.text: A rater whose labels count double
choices.why: No rater counts double here.

choices.text: A real reply with its verdict, beside the rule
choices.why: Right. It settles in one line what a definition leaves open.

prompt: Version 2 passes the agreed refusal for relevance. Where is a wrong refusal caught?

choices.text: In faithfulness, which the judge grades
choices.why: A refusal claims nothing, so it is always faithful.

choices.text: Nowhere: a refusal is always safe
choices.why: A wrong refusal is a wrong answer.

choices.text: In correctness, against the facts
choices.why: Right. Lesson 8 measured it against the expected facts.

choices.text: In the thumbs of the customers
choices.why: The thumbs are a signal, not the criterion.

prompt: Against version 2, on how many of the 60 replies did Ana and Bruno disagree?
Put the steps of the labelling round in the order the lesson took them.
items: measure kappa and read the disagreements
label again and settle what is left

prompt: Settling the disagreements that remain by discussion, and recording the result as its own set, is called ___.
Why did judge-1 fail every refusal for relevance?

choices.text: Its prompt tells it to fail refusals
choices.why: The prompt says nothing about refusals.

choices.text: A refusal shares no words with the question
choices.why: Right. Its similarity to the question is low, and that is all judge-1 measures.

choices.text: A refusal has no citation to check
choices.why: Citations are not part of relevance.

choices.text: The rubric version 2 says it should
choices.why: Version 2 says a refusal passes.

prompt: With refusals passed by rule, the judge agreed on 88.3% and kappa was 0.00. What does that mean?

choices.text: The judge never caught one irrelevant reply
choices.why: Right. Every reply it was sent, it passed.

choices.text: The judge is right on 88% of replies and can be trusted
choices.why: A judge passing everything would reach the same 88%.

choices.text: The labels are wrong on 12% of replies
choices.why: The labels rest on a kappa of 0.86 between people.

choices.text: The refusal rule made the judge worse
choices.why: It removed the commonest disagreement and saved 24 calls.

prompt: What was judge-1's relevance pass rate in lesson 9 really counting?

choices.text: Replies about the wrong subject
choices.why: It passed every one of those it saw.

choices.text: Replies that leaked personal data
choices.why: That is lesson 8's rule, not the judge.

choices.text: Customers who gave a thumbs down
choices.why: The judge never sees the thumbs.

choices.text: The refusals
choices.why: Right. Every one of the 348 replies it failed was the refusal.

prompt: With --refusals-pass, how many of the 60 replies were sent to judge-1?
Match each comparison to its kappa.
A new judge prompt is proposed. What does the team check first?

choices.text: Its pass rate on the week's traffic
choices.why: A pass rate moves for reasons nobody can name until the judge is measured.

choices.text: Its cost per call against judge-1
choices.why: Cost matters after it is known to agree.

choices.text: Whether Ana and Bruno like the wording
choices.why: Liking is not a measure.

choices.text: Its kappa against the same sixty agreed labels
choices.why: Right. A new prompt is a new instrument.

prompt: Two people reach a kappa of 0.5 with each other. What can a judge's kappa against either be expected to reach?

choices.text: Well above 0.5, since a judge is consistent
choices.why: Consistency with one reading is not agreement with the rubric.

choices.text: About 0.5 at best
choices.why: Right. Agreement between people is the practical ceiling.

choices.text: Exactly 1, once its prompt is tuned
choices.why: Tuning to one rater fits that rater's reading.

choices.text: Nothing, kappa is not defined for a judge
choices.why: Any two sets of labels have a kappa.

prompt: Under version 1, how many of the 60 replies did Ana pass?
